ana_01.label: Catalog asymmetry: 391 vs 132
ana_01.content: The two artists are presented as peers but the data is structurally asymmetric. Beyoncé's lyric file contains 22,616 individual lines spread across 391 distinct song entries (including remixes, live cuts, medleys and a Lemonade film script). Taylor Swift's file contains 132 songs total, each as a single Lyrics blob, across 8 studio albums. After splitting Taylor's blobs into lines, Taylor totals 6,955 lyric lines — Beyoncé has 3.3 times as many lines on file. This is not because Beyoncé writes 3x as much per song; it is because her dataset includes every remix and live performance, while Taylor's is one canonical version per studio track.

calculation.output:
beyonce_lyrics: rows=22616, cols=6
taylor_swift_lyrics: rows=132, cols=4
sales: rows=48, cols=8
charts: rows=140, cols=8
Beyonce unique songs: 391
Beyonce avg lines per song: 57.8
Taylor songs: 132
Taylor unique albums: 8

data_table.description: Catalog scale comparison: songs, lines, words per artist

ana_02.label: Taylor's per-album line counts
ana_02.content: Taylor Swift's eight studio albums grow steadily denser through the 2010s before pulling back on folklore. The self-titled debut averages 38.1 lines per song; reputation peaks at 64.5 lines per song before Lover (56.6) and folklore (48.9) trim the form. Total words rise from 3,957 on the debut to a 1989/reputation/Lover plateau just under 7,000 each, then drop to 4,856 on folklore — the shortest record since the debut, and the first signal that something has changed in 2020.

data_table.description: Per-album line and word counts, Taylor Swift's 8 studio albums

ana_03.label: Beyoncé's longest 'songs' are actually films and live shows
ana_03.content: Six of the ten longest entries in Beyoncé's lyric table are not pop songs at all — the longest is the 336-line script of the Lemonade film. Three entries are different live or remix versions of 'Get Me Bodied' (245, 195, and 195 lines), and the second-longest is a 253-line transcript of her 2014 VMAs medley. The first canonical solo studio track to appear in the top 10 by line count is 'That's How You Like It' (122 lines) with Jay-Z. This is a clue that Beyoncé's dataset has been padded out with performance and visual-album material that Taylor's, by construction, does not include.

ana_04.label: Signature hooks: 48 'how you like it's vs 12 'getaway car's
ana_04.content: When you ask each artist's lyric file 'what is the most-repeated single line within one song?', the answers describe two completely different songwriting modes. Beyoncé's top within-song repeat is 'That's how you like it, huh' — sung 48 times in a single track. Six of her top 15 most-repeated lines are 'If I let you go' (20 times each across multiple Ring The Alarm versions), and 'Who run the world? Girls!' takes the next three slots. Taylor's top within-song repeat is 12 — 'Look what you just made me do' (Look What You Made Me Do), 'Come back, be here', 'I'd never walk Cornelia Street again', 'Welcome to New York', 'In a getaway car', all tied. Beyoncé builds songs out of a single chant; Taylor caps her hooks at 12 because there is always another verse to come.

Beyonce top: That's how you like it, huh — 48 (That's How You Like It)
Beyonce 2nd: Who run the world? Girls! — 38 (Run the World remix)
Taylor top: Look what you just made me do — 12 (Look What You Made Me Do)
Taylor 2nd: Come back, be here — 12 (Red)

ana_05.label: Top non-stopword vocabulary
ana_05.content: Strip the function words and pronouns from each artist's catalog and a vocabulary footprint emerges. Beyoncé's top six content words are 'love' (1,362), 'baby' (1,024), 'see' (798), 'girl' (592), 'come' (566), 'want' (551). Taylor's top six are 'love' (248), 'never' (294), 'time' (225), 'back' (240), 'one' (178), 'say' (176). Both share 'love' and 'never' near the top — but Beyoncé's most distinctive frequent words ('baby', 'girl', 'boy', 'feel') run on body and presence, while Taylor's distinctive ones ('time', 'never', 'back', 'said') run on memory and reported speech. 'Halo' alone is sung 383 times across her dataset.

calculation.output:
Beyoncé top: love=1362, baby=1024, see=798, girl=592, come=566, want=551
Taylor top: never=294, love=248, back=240, time=225, one=178, say=176

ana_06.label: Beyoncé's lyrics are denser with love-words
ana_06.content: Beyoncé's lyrics are denser with classical 'love-words' (love, loved, loving, heart, baby, kiss) than Taylor Swift's. After removing stop-words and common filler, 2,925 of Beyoncé's 83,462 content tokens (3.50%) are love-words. Of Taylor's 23,596 content tokens, 556 (2.36%) are. Beyoncé's love-word rate is 1.5x Taylor's — the opposite of the popular framing of Taylor as the relationship songwriter. Taylor talks *about* love and breakups; Beyoncé writes inside the act, with a vocabulary saturated by physical presence ('baby' alone appears 1,024 times in her catalog).

calculation.output:
Beyonce love-words: 2925/83462 = 3.50%
Taylor love-words: 556/23596 = 2.36%
Ratio Beyoncé/Taylor: 1.48x

data_table.description: Love-word density (love/loved/heart/baby/kiss family) per artist, after stop-word removal

ana_07.label: Worldwide sales — Taylor's six vs Beyoncé's five
ana_07.content: On the worldwide-units row of the sales table, Taylor's six reported albums add up to 40.8 million units; Beyoncé's five reported albums add up to 34.5 million. The headline 'Taylor outsells Beyoncé worldwide by 6.3 million' is real — but on a per-album basis the gap nearly disappears: Taylor averages 6.80 million WW units per reported album, Beyoncé 6.90 million. Beyoncé's debut Dangerously in Love is the single largest-selling album in either catalog at 11.0 million worldwide units. Taylor's largest is Fearless (2008) at 12.0 million, narrowly beating it.

Beyoncé WW total: 34.50M (Dangerously 11.0, B'Day 8.0, I Am Sasha Fierce 8.0, Beyoncé 5.0, Lemonade 2.5)

ana_08.label: US sales — Taylor leads 31.7M to 17.7M
ana_08.content: Inside the US specifically, Taylor Swift's six US-row albums sum to 31.66 million units; Beyoncé's six sum to 17.66 million — Taylor leads by 79%. Fearless (7.18M) is the largest US album in either catalog. Beyoncé's Dangerously in Love (5.10M) is fourth — behind Fearless, 1989, and Taylor Swift's self-titled debut. Lemonade, despite winning Album of the Year-tier acclaim, only reached 1.55 million US units in this dataset.

ana_10.label: #1 hit-rate by country — who owns where
ana_10.content: Looking at the rate at which each artist's albums hit #1 in each country, the picture is regional. In the US, Beyoncé hits #1 with 100% of her six albums; Taylor with 87.5% of her eight (one debut missed). In Australia and New Zealand, the order flips: Taylor hits #1 in 75% of AUS releases (vs Beyoncé's 33%) and 87.5% of NZ releases (vs Beyoncé's 17%). Canada belongs to Taylor (87.5% vs 50%). France is no one's country — both artists have 0% #1 albums there. Across every country, Taylor's overall #1 rate is 49.4% of chart entries vs Beyoncé's 38.3%; but country-by-country, Beyoncé dominates in the US and a few specific markets, Taylor dominates the broader anglophone world.

ana_11.label: Album-level chart trajectories
ana_11.content: Plotting the median peak chart position across the ten national charts for each album reveals a steady arc for Taylor and a U-shape for Beyoncé. Taylor's debut median peak is 38; by Red (2012) she is at median peak of 1.0 and stays at 1.0 for every subsequent album through folklore (2020). Beyoncé starts at median peak 1.5 with Dangerously in Love (2003), rises to 4.0 (B'Day) and 4.5 (I Am... Sasha Fierce) — her biggest US-sales era is also her *worst* relative international performance — and then improves again to 2.0, 2.0, and finally 1.0 with Lemonade in 2016.

calculation.output:
Beyoncé: Dangerously 1.5, B'Day 4.0, Sasha Fierce 4.5, 4 2.0, Beyoncé 2.0, Lemonade 1.0
Taylor: Taylor Swift 38, Fearless 6, Speak Now 6, Red 1.0, 1989 1.0, Reputation 1.0, Lover 1.0, Folklore 1.0

ana_12.label: Per-album worldwide units are nearly tied
ana_12.content: If you correct for the fact that Taylor has six worldwide-row albums in the data and Beyoncé has five, the per-album average units sold is essentially identical: 6.80 million for Taylor versus 6.90 million for Beyoncé. The popular framing 'Taylor sold more albums than Beyoncé' is technically true at the catalog level but only because she released more of them in this window. On a per-release basis, both artists sold roughly the same number of copies worldwide.

ana_13.label: Folklore is the only Taylor Swift album that goes net-negative
ana_13.content: Scoring each Taylor Swift album by (positive words − negative words) / total words × 100, every single album from 2006 through 2019 lands net-positive: the debut (+0.88), Fearless (+0.99), Speak Now (+1.02), Red (+0.92), 1989 (+0.77), reputation (+0.45), Lover (+0.41). Folklore, released in 2020 and written during lockdown, is the first and only Taylor Swift album to cross zero into net-negative sentiment: −0.21. The collapse is not noise — folklore has 140 positive words against 150 negative words, in 4,856 total words; every prior album has positive count exceeding negative. Speak Now (2010) is the most positive album she has made; folklore is the only sad one.

data_table.description: Per-album sentiment score (pos% - neg%) for Taylor Swift's 8 studio albums, in release order

ana_14.label: Beyoncé's catalog is +1.63 — overall positive
ana_14.content: Across all 165,050 tokens of Beyoncé's lyric file, 5,605 are positive (3.40%) and 2,917 are negative (1.77%). Net sentiment score is +1.63, placing Beyoncé's full catalog above every Taylor Swift album except Speak Now (+1.02), Fearless (+0.99) and Red (+0.92) — and far above folklore. The popular framing of Beyoncé as 'the artist of breakup albums' (Lemonade especially) is misleading at the catalog level: the positive-word density of love and celebration material on B'Day, 4, and parts of Beyoncé self-titled balances the heaviness elsewhere.

ana_15.label: Words that uniquely belong to each artist
ana_15.content: Using a log-likelihood ratio over the two artists' shared vocabulary, the most-distinctively-Beyoncé content words are 'bodied' (205 times in Beyoncé, 0 in Taylor), 'halo' (383 vs 1), 'slay' (148 vs 0), 'diva' (110 vs 0), 'ladies' (269 vs 2), 'upgrade' (86 vs 0), 'que' (101 vs 0). The most-distinctively-Taylor words are 'starlight' (22 vs 0), 'getaway' (21 vs 0), 'wonderland' (21 vs 0), 'woods' (38 vs 1), 'daylight' (40 vs 2), 'dancing' (48 vs 4), 'york' (38 vs 3), 'darling' (30 vs 5). Beyoncé's distinctive vocabulary names the body and the room ('bodied', 'ladies', 'diva'); Taylor's names landscapes and times of day ('starlight', 'wonderland', 'woods', 'daylight').

Beyoncé-leaning: bodied 205/0, halo 383/1, slay 148/0, ladies 269/2, diva 110/0
Taylor-leaning: starlight 0/22, wonderland 0/21, getaway 0/21, woods 1/38, daylight 2/40, dancing 4/48, york 3/38

caveats.content: Beyoncé's lyric file includes remixes, live versions, medleys, and a Lemonade film script. Taylor's contains one canonical version per song. Direct line/word counts are not apples-to-apples without filtering.

Sentiment scoring uses a curated subset of Bing positive/negative words (~200 entries) rather than the full 6,800-word lexicon. The rank ordering across albums matches the published tidytext analysis style (Speak Now/Fearless top, folklore bottom) but absolute scores differ from tidytext::get_sentiments("bing").

Sentiment lexicons systematically misread Black Vernacular English and slang. 'Bad' meaning 'good', 'killing it', 'sick' as praise — these all score negative. So Beyoncé's sentiment numbers may understate the positive valence of her actual material.

Sales figures come from each artist's Wikipedia discography page, which aggregates from labels, RIAA certifications, and IFPI press releases. They are not RIAA-audited point-of-sale numbers; rank ordering is reliable, precise dollar values are not.

Beyoncé's worldwide row is labelled 'World' (5 albums); Taylor's is labelled 'WW' (6 albums). Cross-artist worldwide totals require joining on different country codes — a quirk of the source scrape, not a feature of the music.
